title: Tournament tree — second smallest
label: idb
statement:
A tournament tree is a binary tree where every parent contains the minimum of its two children.

Leaves have unique values.

Find the second smallest value.

Explain why the second smallest must appear among the nodes that lost directly to the minimum.

flaw.ctx: You asked for the second smallest value in a tournament tree.
flaw.answer: It only looks at the root's two children. The runner-up lost to the minimum at **some** level on the minimum's path — not necessarily the top. On the stated tree it returns 7, not 5.
flaw.fix: Walk down the path the minimum took and take the smallest opponent along it — O(height).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> A tournament tree is a binary tree where every parent contains the minimum of its two children.
> 
> Leaves have unique values.
> 
> Find the second smallest value.
> 
> Explain why the second smallest must appear among the nodes that lost directly to the minimum.

A knockout tournament, stored as a tree. Every internal node holds the winner of the match between its two children, and winning means being smaller. The overall winner is at the root. Who came second?

The second smallest **leaf** value. Equivalently, the second smallest distinct value in the tree — they are the same, because every internal value is a copy of some leaf value.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Internal nodes have two children; leaves have none. | A single-child internal node would break "minimum of its two children". The code guards against it anyway, because a malformed tree should not produce a plausible wrong answer. |
| Leaf values are unique, as stated. | This is load-bearing. With duplicate leaves, two children could both equal the parent and the winner’s path would fork — the walk-down approach would have to branch, or you fall back to O(n). |
| "Second smallest" means the runner-up leaf, not the second smallest node. | Every internal value duplicates a leaf value, so the second smallest **distinct** value in the whole tree equals the second smallest leaf. Worth confirming, because "second smallest node" could be read as the minimum again. |
| At least two leaves. | One leaf has no runner-up. Throwing is more honest than returning a sentinel that could be a real value. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The statement asks you to justify the insight, so here is the justification, which is the answer.

Call the minimum `m`. Take any leaf `x` other than `m`. Because `m` reached the root, `m` won every match on its path. Now trace `x` upward: it keeps winning until it meets the path of `m`, and at that point it loses — either directly to `m`, or to something that itself lost to `m` further up.

If `x` lost directly to `m`, it is a candidate. If `x` lost to some other value `y` first, then `y < x`, and `y` went on to lose to `m`. So `y` is smaller than `x` and is *also* not the minimum — which means `x` is at best **third**. Therefore the second smallest can only be a value that faced `m` directly.

That gives the algorithm: walk from the root down the winner’s path, and at each step the sibling is one of the values that lost to `m`. There are exactly `h` of them, so the answer is `min` over the h siblings — O(h) time, O(1) space. On a perfect tournament of n leaves that is O(log n), against O(n) for scanning every node.

Two details that make the walk work. The winner’s path is identifiable because the parent equals exactly one child — **unique leaves is what guarantees "exactly"**, and it is the reason that constraint is in the statement. And the siblings are exactly the losers, because a match is a parent with two children and the one that did not become the parent lost it.

The reason LeetCode rates its version Easy is that it accepts an O(n) traversal looking for the smallest value greater than the root. Same answer, and it throws away the structure — which is precisely what this statement is asking you not to do.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Traverse every node, collect the values, and return the second smallest distinct one. Or collect all the leaves and sort them. *O(n) traversal, or O(n log n) with a sort. O(n) space for the collection, or O(1) if you track the best two as you go.*

**Why not good enough.** It is correct, it is what LeetCode 671 accepts, and it is worth stating as the baseline. It is also the answer that ignores the one thing you were told about the input. The tree is not an arbitrary bag of numbers — it is the record of a tournament, and that record already contains the answer along a single path. Scanning n nodes to find something that h comparisons will give you is the difference between using the structure and merely visiting it. On a tournament of a million players that is 20 comparisons against a million.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | The root of a tournament tree |
| TRANSFORMATION | The winner’s path from root to leaf is identified by following the child whose value equals its parent |
| DATA STRUCTURE | None — one running minimum and one pointer |
| ALGORITHM | Walk down the winner’s path; at each step take the minimum of the sibling values |
| OUTPUT | The smallest value that lost directly to the minimum |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Reject a null root, and reject a lone leaf — no runner-up exists.
- Start at the root with `best = int.MaxValue`.
- While the current node has children: identify which child equals the current value — that is the winner; the other is the loser.
- `best = min(best, loser.Value)`.
- Move to the winner and repeat.
- Return `best`.

- Leaf values are **unique**, which is what makes the winner’s path unambiguous.
- Every internal node holds the minimum of its children, so the root is the global minimum.
- At least two leaves are needed for an answer to exist.
- The tree need not be perfect, though a tournament usually is.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| No data structure at all | Worth saying. The answer is a walk with two variables, and reaching for a heap or a list is the reflex to resist. |
| Following the child equal to the parent | The parent is the minimum of its children, so it equals one of them. Unique leaves means exactly one — so the path is well defined and needs no search. |
| `best` as a running minimum over the siblings | There are h candidates and only the smallest matters, so nothing needs storing. |
| Iterative rather than recursive | It is a single path, so there is no branching to recurse over. A `while` loop is both shorter and immune to stack depth on a degenerate tree. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`cur.Left.Value == cur.Value` picks the winner.** The parent holds the minimum of its children, so it equals one of them. Because leaves are unique, no two internal nodes can carry the same value from different leaves, so exactly one child matches and the path never forks. **If leaves could repeat, this line would silently pick the left one** and the walk could follow the wrong path — which is why the uniqueness constraint is in the statement and worth repeating back.

**`while (cur.Left != null || cur.Right != null)`.** Either-or rather than both, deliberately. A well-formed tournament node has two children, but a malformed one might have one, and this condition still terminates rather than dereferencing null. The `if (loser != null)` inside then skips the missing sibling instead of crashing.

**`best` starts at `int.MaxValue`.** And is guaranteed to be overwritten, because the guard has already established that at least one match exists. Without that guard, returning `int.MaxValue` from a single-leaf tree would be a wrong answer disguised as a real one — which is why the throw is better than a sentinel.

**Why this is O(h) and not O(n).** The loop advances to one child per iteration and never branches, so it touches exactly one node per level. Every other node in the tree is skipped, and the justification for skipping them is the argument in the observation — the code is short precisely because the reasoning was done first.

**Throwing for a single leaf.** `InvalidOperationException` rather than returning `int.MaxValue` or -1. A sentinel cannot be distinguished from a real value, and for a function whose whole job is to return a value, "there is no answer" is genuinely exceptional.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SecondSmallest` | O(h) | O(1) | One node per level, two variables |
| on a perfect tournament | O(log n) | O(1) | h = log₂(n) for n leaves |
| brute-force scan | O(n) | O(1) | Every node visited — the baseline to beat |

**h, not log n, is the honest bound.** The statement does not promise a balanced tree, and a degenerate one has h = n, at which point the walk is no better than the scan. For a real tournament the tree is perfect by construction and it is O(log n) — but writing O(log n) without the balance assumption is the kind of imprecision worth avoiding, especially when the neighbouring question on this page (Q10) hands you an explicitly imbalanced tree.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Null root | Throws `ArgumentNullException`. |
| Single leaf | Throws — no runner-up exists. |
| Two leaves | One comparison; the loser is the answer. |
| Runner-up adjacent to the winner | Found on the last step of the walk. |
| Runner-up at the top of the tree | Found on the first step. My second example — the answer is 3, at depth 1, while 50 sits next to the winner and is not the answer. |
| Duplicate leaf values | **Outside the stated constraints.** The winner’s path could fork and the walk may pick the wrong branch. The fallback is the O(n) scan; say so rather than claiming the walk still works. |
| Imbalanced tree | Correct, but O(h) = O(n) in the worst case. |
| Malformed node with one child | Handled defensively: the loop still terminates and the missing sibling is skipped. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Explain why the second smallest must appear among the nodes that lost directly to the minimum.**

Let `m` be the minimum and let `x` be any other leaf. Trace `x` upward: it wins until it meets `m`’s path, where it loses. Either it loses directly to `m`, in which case it is a candidate; or it first loses to some `y ≠ m`, which means `y < x`, and `y` later loses to `m`. Then `m < y < x`, so `x` is at least third. Hence only the direct losers to `m` can be second, and there are exactly `h` of them — one per level of `m`’s path.

*Trade-off:* None; it is the justification. Note what it depends on: that the tournament is a genuine knockout, so every non-winner loses exactly once and to a strictly smaller value. Change the tournament to best-of-three, or allow a losing value to continue, and the argument fails immediately.

**Find the third smallest.**

The third smallest is **not** simply the second smallest of the h direct losers. Suppose `s` is the runner-up. The third smallest is either another direct loser to `m`, or it is something that lost directly to `s` on `s`’s own path back down to its leaf. So you need `m`’s losers **plus** `s`’s losers — which means locating `s`’s leaf and walking its subtree path.

Generalising to the k-th, this becomes the classic **tournament selection**: repeatedly remove the current winner and replay only the affected path, which is O(k log n) overall and is exactly how a selection tree works.

*Trade-off:* O(h) for the second, O(k log n) for the k-th. Beyond a fairly small k the O(n) scan with a bounded heap wins, and the crossover is around k ≈ n / log n. The valuable part of this answer is recognising that the clean structure of the second-smallest argument does not simply extend — candidates who assume it does give a confidently wrong algorithm.

**Duplicate leaf values are allowed now.**

With duplicates, a parent can equal **both** children, so the winner’s path forks and "follow the child equal to the parent" is no longer well defined. Also "second smallest" becomes ambiguous: the second smallest *distinct* value, or the second element of the sorted multiset (which could equal the minimum)?

The robust answer is to fall back to an O(n) traversal tracking the two smallest distinct values. Attempting to fix the walk means exploring both branches at every tie, which in the worst case — all leaves equal — degenerates to O(n) anyway, with considerably more code.

*Trade-off:* O(n) instead of O(h), and it is the correct trade rather than a defeat: the structure genuinely stops carrying enough information. Saying "the constraint was doing real work and here is exactly which line it supported" is the answer being looked for.

**Return who the runner-up lost to, and the match path.**

Record the node where `best` was updated. Everything on the winner’s path from the root down to that point is the sequence of matches the runner-up would have had to win, and the runner-up lost to the minimum at that node. Collect the path into a list as you walk.

*Trade-off:* O(h) extra space for the path, which is nothing. It is also the more useful API for anything actually displaying a tournament bracket, and it is free because the walk already visits exactly those nodes.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *A single leaf? Duplicate leaves?* — No second smallest → throw; the statement says unique

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Why O(height)?* — Only the opponents of the minimum can be second
